query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lowering the Cu content in FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings reduces the high-temperature wear rate by diminishing tensile-compression asymmetry tied to enhanced nano-twinning and dislocation slip differences at the coating–substrate interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating (baseline composition, e.g., one similar to Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13) applied on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Modify the baseline composition by reducing the Cu fraction (for example, by substituting part of the Cu with Fe) to lower the alloy’s propensity for nano-twinning and the associated tensile-compression asymmetry.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear conditions, e.g., operating at temperatures around 400–600 °C under high load sliding or contact stress representative of service conditions for protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural integrity of the coating–substrate interface, particularly the density and distribution of deformation features such as twinning and dislocation slip zones.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, increased Cu content enhances tensile-compression asymmetry by promoting nano-twinning during compression and reducing dislocation slip during tension. This results in localized strain and stress concentrations at the coating–substrate interface. Reducing the Cu content shifts the balance of deformation mechanisms, leading to more uniform plastic deformation and less wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature, high-load conditions, coatings with reduced Cu content will display a lower wear rate, decreased evidence of strain localization (fewer nano-twins relative to dislocation activity), and overall improved integrity of the coating–substrate interface compared to the baseline composition.
generation.baseline: Standard FeNiCrCoCu coating with a higher Cu content (e.g., Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13) that exhibits increased tensile-compression asymmetry and corresponding wear under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to thin-film protective coatings on conventional metals operating at temperatures roughly between 400–600 °C and under high mechanical loads. It may not hold at room temperature or under low-load conditions where different wear mechanisms prevail.
generation.uncertainty: While molecular dynamics and machine learning studies suggest a role of Cu content in tensile-compression asymmetry, it is uncertain how these deformation mechanisms directly translate to wear performance in an actual high-temperature environment. Other factors such as oxidation or substrate-induced stress might also play a role.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of thin-film coatings on identical conventional metal substrates. One set will use the baseline FeNiCrCoCu composition and the other will use the modified, Cu-reduced composition. Subject both groups to controlled high-temperature wear testing at 500 °C under high load conditions. Microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM for detecting nano-twinning and dislocation features) and wear rate measurements (e.g., volume loss or friction coefficient changes) will be performed.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss or mass loss) under high load at 500 °C
Microstructural characterization (nano-twin density, dislocation patterns, coating–substrate interface integrity)
Quantitative analysis of tensile-compression asymmetry indicators from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-reduced coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear rate combined with a decrease in tensile-compression asymmetry and strain localization compared to the baseline coatings, the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractCompared with traditional alloys, high-entropy alloys have better mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. However, their mechanical properties and microstructural evolution behavior are unclear due to their complex composition. Machine learning has powerful data processing and analysis capabilities, that provides technical advantages for in-depth study of the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. Thus, we combined machine learning and molecular dynamics to predict the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys. The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa. Furthermore, molecular dynamics is used to verify the predicted mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, and it is found that the error between the tensile strength predicted by machine learning and the tensile strength obtained by molecular dynamics simulation is within 0.5%.
